# Forensic Dossier — Nexi S.p.A. (NEXI.MI)

*Italy's largest payments processor — card issuing, merchant acquiring (point-of-sale and e-commerce), and digital-banking infrastructure, built from the SIA and Nets mergers. Four consecutive earnings calls reviewed: November 2024 (nine-month 2024), February 2025 (full-year 2024), May 2025 (first-quarter 2025), and November 2025 (nine-month 2025).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these four calls the story shifts in a very specific, telling direction: **from a growth-and-margin story to a cash-return-and-deleveraging story.** That is the single most important arc here.

In late 2024 (nine-month call) the headline was "continued delivery of growth and margin expansion" — revenue up 5.6% year-to-date, merchant solutions up 6.9%, with a long lecture on the "structural long-term growth drivers" of merchant services (the secular shift from cash to digital, customer-base growth, customer-value management). Management spent most of the call teaching analysts why the top line should compound at "mid-to-high single digit."

By the February 2025 full-year call, the lead message had already moved. The first words were "continued delivery of growth and **most importantly, strong acceleration of cash generation.**" Management introduced the capital-return program — the first-ever dividend (€300 million) plus a €300 million buyback, €600 million total, an implied yield "more than 10%." Growth was still there (5.1% for the year) but it had been demoted; cash and the path to investment-grade had been promoted.

By November 2025 (the most recent call), the arc completes. Reported revenue growth has collapsed to **2.8% for nine months and just 1.8% in the quarter**, with merchant solutions up a bare 0.6% in the quarter. Management's defense is the "underlying growth, net of this effect, is at about 6%" — the "effect" being bank-contract losses and price renegotiations that they now say "will peak probably in Q4 this year." The pitch is now almost entirely: deleveraging (net debt down to 2.6x EBITDA), €1.1 billion returned across 2024-2025, and "more than €800 million" of excess cash. Growth has become a footnote defended by adjustment.

The quietly-fading driver: the bullish cash-to-digital penetration math ("1 to 2 percentage points per year… for the very, very, very long term"). It is still asserted but the conviction has drained, and analysts are now openly asking whether "this has taken its course."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Continued delivery of profitable growth," mid-to-high-single-digit structural | Reported revenue: +5.1% FY24, then decelerating to **2.8% / 1.8% by 9M-2025**; the screener shows **-0.3% revenue YoY** and a 3-year revenue CAGR of ~4.9% | **Diverges.** The reported top line has stalled. The "6% underlying" is real but it is a management-defined number that strips out contractual losses they themselves signed up to. |
| "Strong acceleration of cash generation," >€800m excess cash | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of **€1.21 billion**; price-to-free-cash-flow of just **5x**; free-cash-flow margin ~12.8%; free cash flow +52.9% year-on-year | **Matches — and is the real story.** The cash is genuine. This is a cash machine trading at a distressed multiple. |
| "We continue to create value for shareholders," €1.1bn returned, dividend growing | Confirmed in the transcripts (€600m in 2025, +20%); but note book value per share has compounded **-19.5% over five years** | **Matches on cash return, but the equity base is shrinking.** Returns are funded partly by buying back stock and the book value is being hollowed by goodwill write-downs. |
| EBITDA margin "north of 57%" | Net margin is **-53.8%** and reported net income was **-€3.38 billion in 2025** (EPS -2.75); return on equity -10.8%, return on invested capital just **1.9%** | **The gap is the whole forensic case.** The 57% is a margin on earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA); the catastrophic net loss is driven by the amortization and impairment of the enormous goodwill from the SIA/Nets deals. Cash earnings are strong; accounting earnings are deeply negative. A return on invested capital of 1.9% says the acquired empire does not yet earn its cost of capital. |
| Deleveraging "towards 2 to 2.5x" | Net debt of roughly **€917 million** (recomputed: €6.78bn total debt minus €5.87bn cash); Altman-Z solvency score **0.6** (distress zone) | **Mixed.** Leverage on an EBITDA basis is improving and is investment-grade rated, but the screener's solvency flag is in the danger band because of the negative net income and goodwill-heavy balance sheet. |

The pattern: **everything management says about cash is true; everything implied about the quality and durability of growth is generous.** The 2025 reported -2.75 EPS and -€3.38bn net loss are an accounting event (goodwill), not a cash event — but they are also a confession that the merger-built business has not yet generated the returns that justified the purchase prices.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining — and shifting from offense to defense.**

- **November 2024:** Offensive, teaching mode. "Structural drivers that are really, really, really visible and strong." Confident enough to *choose* the deep-dive topic (merchant growth drivers).
- **February 2025:** Still confident but the centre of gravity moves to capital structure. The "formula" language (top-line growth, operating leverage, cash leverage) is a sign they are reframing the story around what they *can* control.
- **May 2025:** Defensive notes creep in — "despite some effect from the leap year and the different Easter phasing," explaining away a soft 3.7% print. The chosen deep-dive is now "debt and capital structure management," not growth.
- **November 2025:** Fully defensive. The quarter is "significantly impacted by discontinuities," the gap between reported (1.8%) and "underlying" (6%) is "widening," and the reassurance is that the damage "will peak probably in Q4." When the story becomes "trust the adjusted number and wait for the headwind to peak," confidence has declined.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** Management has a genuinely good record of hitting the numbers it chooses to guide on — the cash targets in particular. They guided €717m excess cash for 2024 and delivered it; they guided ">€800m" for 2025 and reiterated it "with a high degree of confidence." The dividend and buyback were promised and paid.

But two things temper this. First, the screener shows an earnings-beat rate of just **1 of 7 quarters (14%)** — they miss the consensus earnings line far more than they beat it, which fits a company that guides conservatively on cash but cannot control the accounting result. Second, and more damning, the revenue trajectory has serially disappointed: the "5-6%" underlying growth framing from early 2025 became 1.8% reported by year-end, rescued only by an adjustment for "discontinuities" whose magnitude clearly grew on them ("more material effects… as we go" than first anticipated). Reliability on cash: high. Reliability on growth: low.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring, unresolved analyst worry is **whether the cash-to-digital growth engine is exhausted.** Deutsche Bank's analyst put it directly in February 2025: "we get a lot of questions on this one that this has taken its course, and maybe we are now thinking of 1% to 2% per year." Management's answer ("the 1 to 2 percentage points per year still remains a good measure") effectively conceded the deceleration.

The second pressure point is **bank-contract losses in Italy** — analysts kept probing the impact of Banco BPM, Cassa Centrale and the wave of Italian bank M&A (Credit Agricole/BPM, BPM/Monte dei Paschi/Mediobanca). Management's answers grew more defensive over the four calls as the "discontinuities" they downplayed in 2024 ("low single-digit millions… irrelevant") became "the highest impact we've had year-to-date" by November 2025.

The third is **competition from single-platform SME fintechs** (the SumUp/Adyen/newer-player threat). Management's repeated rebuttal is the German market-share story ("merchant solutions in Germany is growing double-digit… we can compete, we can win"). It is a real proof point, but it is also the one geography they cite over and over, which is itself a tell.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Reported revenue growth has decelerated from ~5% to under 2% while the gap to "underlying" growth keeps widening — the adjustment is doing more and more work (Nov-2025).
🔴 Return on invested capital of just 1.9% and a five-year book-value-per-share decline of ~19.5% — the merger empire is not earning its cost of capital, and the equity base is eroding (screener financials).
🔴 The €3.38bn 2025 net loss and the 0.6 Altman-Z solvency score sit on a goodwill-stuffed balance sheet vulnerable to further impairment.
🔴 Italian bank consolidation is an open-ended threat to the distribution relationships that feed the merchant and issuing books (Nov-2025 Q&A); a large Nordic client is in-sourcing its processing.
🟢 Trailing free cash flow of €1.21bn against a ~€4.6bn equity value — a free-cash-flow yield well above 20%, and the cash is being returned (dividend plus buyback) and used to deleverage to investment-grade.
🟢 Germany merchant solutions growing double-digit / mid-teens — proof the franchise can take share even against newer SME-focused platforms (Nov-2025).
🟢 Disciplined, accretive-only M&A and active portfolio rationalization (Digital Banking Solutions disposals) — management is shrinking to quality rather than empire-building.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most revealing terminology shift is the rise of the word **"underlying."** In 2024 management talked about reported growth; by late 2025 nearly every growth statement is qualified — "underlying growth, net of this effect, is at about 6%." When a management team trains analysts to look past the printed number to a self-defined adjusted one, the printed number has stopped cooperating.

A second signal: the **in-sourcing by a "large Nordic client"** that management admits was "a decision which goes back 3 or 4 years and has been postponed a number of times" and "is now kicking in." This is a customer taking processing in-house — the precise disintermediation risk that haunts the whole legacy-processor category, and management discloses it almost in passing.

Third, capital-allocation language has quietly hardened toward **return-of-capital over reinvestment** ("return most of the excess cash"), and on M&A management has gone from acquirer to "very low/marginal… probably very small in size." A payments roll-up that has stopped rolling up is signaling its own growth options are thinning.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING** — from a debt-funded growth-by-acquisition processor into a deleveraging, cash-returning utility-like compounder. The pivot is being executed competently (investment-grade achieved, dividend initiated, leverage falling), but it is a pivot *forced by* decelerating organic growth, not chosen from strength.

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: **Is the ~5x free-cash-flow multiple a fear-print on a durable cash machine, or the market correctly pricing a payments incumbent whose take-rate and bank-distribution moat are being slowly disintermediated?** The bull needs only the cash to be durable; the bear needs the 1.9% return on invested capital and the in-sourcing / fintech-disintermediation signals to be the leading edge of terminal decline.

**Economic moat:** NARROW. The moat is a blend of scale-cost (the largest acquiring/issuing platform in Italy and a top-three European processor) and embedded bank-distribution relationships (switching costs for partner banks). But the *evidence* points to erosion, not width: a return on invested capital of 1.9% is far below cost of capital, reported growth has stalled, a major Nordic client is in-sourcing, and Italian bank M&A threatens the very distribution that anchors the moat. Gross margin is high and stable (~58%) and the German share gains are real, which keeps this NARROW rather than NONE — but the return profile says the durable earnings base is not widening.

**Secular threat: material (not yet terminal).** The structural force is payments disintermediation — stablecoin and account-to-account rails, single-platform SME fintechs (SumUp/Adyen-style), and large clients in-sourcing processing — all of which compress take-rates and float for legacy acquirer/issuers. Nexi is partly insulated by its SME focus, its regulated-infrastructure scale, and the still-incomplete cash-to-digital conversion in Italy/Poland/Greece, so this reads as a margin/growth headwind rather than a terminal-value wipeout today. But the 1.9% return on invested capital means there is little cushion if the threat accelerates. The cheapness is therefore *partly* a fear-print and *partly* a structurally-pressured base — a value case that lives or dies on the durability of free cash flow, not on a re-acceleration of growth.

The first words were "continued delivery of growth and **most importantly, strong acceleration of cash generation.**" Management introduced the capital-return program — the first-ever dividend (€300 million) plus a €300 million buyback, €600 million total, an implied yield "more than 10%." By November 2025 (the most recent call), the arc completes. Reported revenue growth has collapsed to **2.8% for nine months and just 1.8% in the quarter**, with merchant solutions up a bare 0.6% in the quarter. The most revealing terminology shift is the rise of the word **"underlying."** In 2024 management talked about reported growth; by late 2025 nearly every growth statement is qualified — "underlying growth, net of this effect, is at about 6%." When a management team trains analysts to look past the printed number to a self-defined adjusted one, the printed number has stopped cooperating.

A second signal: the **in-sourcing by a "large Nordic client"** that management admits was "a decision which goes back 3 or 4 years and has been postponed a number of times" and "is now kicking in." This is a customer taking processing in-house — the precise disintermediation risk that haunts the whole legacy-processor category, and management discloses it almost in passing.

Third, capital-allocation language has quietly hardened toward **return-of-capital over reinvestment** ("return most of the excess cash"), and on M&A management has gone from acquirer to "very low/marginal… probably very small in size." A payments roll-up that has stopped rolling up is signaling its own growth options are thinning.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING** — from a debt-funded growth-by-acquisition processor into a deleveraging, cash-returning utility-like compounder. The pivot is being executed competently (investment-grade achieved, dividend initiated, leverage falling), but it is a pivot *forced by* decelerating organic growth, not chosen from strength.

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: **Is the ~5x free-cash-flow multiple a fear-print on a durable cash machine, or the market correctly pricing a payments incumbent whose take-rate and bank-distribution moat are being slowly disintermediated?** The bull needs only the cash to be durable; the bear needs the 1.9% return on invested capital and the in-sourcing / fintech-disintermediation signals to be the leading edge of terminal decline.

**Economic moat:** NARROW. The moat is a blend of scale-cost (the largest acquiring/issuing platform in Italy and a top-three European processor) and embedded bank-distribution relationships (switching costs for partner banks). But the *evidence* points to erosion, not width: a return on invested capital of 1.9% is far below cost of capital, reported growth has stalled, a major Nordic client is in-sourcing, and Italian bank M&A threatens the very distribution that anchors the moat. Gross margin is high and stable (~58%) and the German share gains are real, which keeps this NARROW rather than NONE — but the return profile says the durable earnings base is not widening.

**Secular threat: material (not yet terminal).** The structural force is payments disintermediation — stablecoin and account-to-account rails, single-platform SME fintechs (SumUp/Adyen-style), and large clients in-sourcing processing — all of which compress take-rates and float for legacy acquirer/issuers. Nexi is partly insulated by its SME focus, its regulated-infrastructure scale, and the still-incomplete cash-to-digital conversion in Italy/Poland/Greece, so this reads as a margin/growth headwind rather than a terminal-value wipeout today. But the 1.9% return on invested capital means there is little cushion if the threat accelerates. The cheapness is therefore *partly* a fear-print and *partly* a structurally-pressured base — a value case that lives or dies on the durability of free cash flow, not on a re-acceleration of growth.

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from five consecutive earnings calls (November 2024 through November 2025) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

Nexi is Italy's dominant payments processor and merchant acquirer — the business that sits between shops and banks and takes a small slice of every card tap. It was assembled through two large mergers (SIA in Italy and Nets in Northern Europe), and the whole story of the last two years is management trying to convince the market that the merged machine throws off large and growing cash while it slowly pays down the debt those deals left behind.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has quietly but decisively contracted over these five quarters.

- **Late 2024 (Nov):** Confident and offensive. Revenue up 5.6% in the first nine months, merchant solutions up 6.9%, and a long lecture on the "structural long-term growth drivers" — cash-to-digital conversion worth "1 to 2 percentage points per year for the very, very, very long term." Management framed the company as a "mid-to-high single digit structural growth" business, with merchant services "towards high-single digit to double digit."
- **Feb 2025 (FY2024):** The pivot to cash. The centerpiece became capital return — the first-ever dividend (€300m) plus a €300m buyback, "10% of the equity value... implied yield of more than 10%." - **Nov 2025 (9M):** The contraction becomes explicit. Reported revenue growth collapsed to +1.8% in the quarter, with management repeatedly separating "reported" from an "underlying ~6%" — the gap being "bank losses from the past and some key bank contract price renegotiation effects" that "will peak probably in Q4." The growth-driver lecture is gone; the call is now about defending the underlying number and pointing to Germany.

The arc is a company that started these quarters selling secular growth and ended them selling *normalized* growth net of a widening list of "extraordinary" contract losses — while the cash-return promise did all the heavy lifting.

# Forensic Dossier — Nexi S.p.A. (NEXI.MI)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from five consecutive earnings calls (November 2024 through November 2025) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

Nexi is Italy's dominant payments processor and merchant acquirer — the business that sits between shops and banks and takes a small slice of every card tap. It was assembled through two large mergers (SIA in Italy and Nets in Northern Europe), and the whole story of the last two years is management trying to convince the market that the merged machine throws off large and growing cash while it slowly pays down the debt those deals left behind.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has quietly but decisively contracted over these five quarters.

- **Late 2024 (Nov):** Confident and offensive. Revenue up 5.6% in the first nine months, merchant solutions up 6.9%, and a long lecture on the "structural long-term growth drivers" — cash-to-digital conversion worth "1 to 2 percentage points per year for the very, very, very long term." Management framed the company as a "mid-to-high single digit structural growth" business, with merchant services "towards high-single digit to double digit."
- **Feb 2025 (FY2024):** The pivot to cash. The centerpiece became capital return — the first-ever dividend (€300m) plus a €300m buyback, "10% of the equity value... implied yield of more than 10%." Investment-grade upgrades from Fitch and S&P. The message shifted from "we grow" to "we generate cash and hand it back."
- **May 2025 (Q1):** Still steady — revenue +3.7% (blamed on leap-year/Easter phasing), EBITDA +7.1%, margin up ~150 basis points. Management leaned on Germany (+9% merchant) as proof it can beat the SoftPOS newcomers.
- **Nov 2025 (9M):** The contraction becomes explicit. Reported revenue growth collapsed to +1.8% in the quarter, with management repeatedly separating "reported" from an "underlying ~6%" — the gap being "bank losses from the past and some key bank contract price renegotiation effects" that "will peak probably in Q4." The growth-driver lecture is gone; the call is now about defending the underlying number and pointing to Germany.

The arc is a company that started these quarters selling secular growth and ended them selling *normalized* growth net of a widening list of "extraordinary" contract losses — while the cash-return promise did all the heavy lifting.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Continued delivery of growth" (every call) | Revenue **−0.3% YoY** on the latest fiscal year (2025 €6.27B vs 2024 €6.29B); 3-yr CAGR +4.9% but decelerating hard | **Diverges.** Reported top line actually went slightly *backwards* in 2025. The "6% underlying" is real but the reported line is flat-to-down. |
| "Strong acceleration of cash generation... more than €800m excess cash" | FCF margin **12.8%**, TTM free cash flow **€1.21B**, FCF +52.9% YoY, P/FCF **5.3x** | **Matches — this is the true anchor.** The cash story is the one claim the numbers fully corroborate. |
| "EBITDA margin expansion" | 9M-2025 margin expansion **35 basis points** — down sharply from the "at least 100bp" delivered in 2024 | **Weakened.** Margin expansion is decelerating, not accelerating. |
| Company earns healthy returns | ROE **−10.8%**, ROIC **1.9%**, net income **−€3.38B** in 2025, EPS **−2.75** | **Diverges violently.** The reported P&L is deeply loss-making — driven by a ~€3.7B non-cash goodwill write-down (verified below). |
| Deleveraging toward 2–2.5x | Net debt **~€917M** (total debt €6.78B minus cash €5.87B, per the live correction); management-quoted leverage 2.8x → 2.6x EBITDA | **Broadly matches.** Leverage is genuinely falling, and the balance-sheet cash pile is large. |
| "We can compete and win" vs SoftPOS newcomers | Germany merchant solutions genuinely **+9% (Q1) to mid-teens (Q3)** | **Matches — the one unambiguous green flag.** |

The core tension: management's *cash* claims are true and its *growth* claims are increasingly qualified. The screener's brutal −53.8% net margin and −2.75 EPS are the goodwill impairment, not operating collapse — but they are the market's visible scoreboard, and they confirm the model-quality problem: Nexi overpaid for SIA and Nets, and 2025 was the year the accountants said so.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining.**

- Nov 2024: offensive, expansive — "very, very, very long term," "shaping Nexi for future profitable growth."
- Feb 2025: pivots to reassurance — "much sharper and much clearer message... of continuity."
- Nov 2025: defensive and hedged — every growth figure now comes with a "but underlying is 6%," and CFO Bernardo Mingrone repeatedly walks analysts through *why the reported number is worse than the business*. The shift from selling the top line to defending it is the clearest tone signal here.

The language migrated from **offense (growth, structural drivers, share gains)** to **defense (efficiency, cost control, underlying-vs-reported bridges, contract-loss management)** over the window.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium — reliable on cash, unreliable on the growth framing.**

Management delivered exactly what it promised on capital return and cash: the 2024 guidance (mid-single-digit revenue, 100bp+ margin, €700m+ excess cash) was met, and the €600m return happened on schedule. That is a real track record.

But the *narrative* guidance repeatedly under-delivered against its own framing. The "mid-to-high single digit structural growth" pitch of late 2024 became +1.8% reported by 9M-2025. Management always had a reason (leap year, Easter, bank losses, project phasing) — the pattern of a widening "extraordinary items" bucket that always explains the gap is itself a yellow flag. The screener's earnings-beat rate of **1 of 7 quarters (14%)** corroborates that management's own forward framing runs optimistic relative to what lands.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Sabadell/BBVA** — pressed on every call ("any news there?"), and management could only say "we read the news as much as you do." This deal *did* later turn into bad news (see §6): it collapsed.
- **SoftPOS / single-platform newcomers** — the recurring "how do you compete with the new SME players" question. Management's answer (Germany) is genuinely strong, but the persistence of the question signals a market that is not convinced the moat holds.
- **Bank contract losses** (Banco BPM, Cassa Centrale, the German issuing client, the Nordic in-sourcing) — analysts kept probing the size and duration; management kept minimizing ("a few million euros here and there") while the cumulative drag grew large enough to flatten reported revenue.
- **Cash-to-digital run-rate** — Deutsche Bank explicitly asked whether the secular tailwind "has taken its course" and is now "1% to 2% per year." Management conceded the lower end. The core secular driver is maturing.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The reported top line went negative** (−0.3% in 2025) as bank-contract losses overwhelmed underlying growth — and management guided this peaks in Q4-2025 and only fades "in the second half of 2026."
🔴 **A ~€3.7B goodwill impairment** drove a −€3.38B net loss and −2.75 EPS — the accounting admission that the SIA/Nets deals were overpriced (verified below).
🔴 **The buyback vanished.** After completing €300m of buybacks in 2025, the forward plan (verified below) dropped repurchases entirely — a message the market read as reduced confidence.
🔴 **Cash-to-digital secular tailwind maturing** to the low end of the 1–2% range.
🔴 **Earnings-beat rate 14%** (1 of 7 quarters) — management's forward framing consistently runs ahead of delivery.

🟢 **Free cash flow is real and large** — €1.21B TTM, 5.3x P/FCF, +52.9% YoY; this is the genuine investment case.
🟢 **Germany is winning share** — mid-teens merchant growth against exactly the newcomers the bears fear.
🟢 **Deleveraging + investment-grade** — leverage 2.8x → 2.6x, upgraded by Fitch and S&P; the balance sheet is de-risking.
🟢 **Piotroski 7/9** — the underlying financial-health screen is solid despite the headline loss.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important tell is the **"underlying vs reported" wedge** that management introduced and then widened. In late 2024 growth was simply "5.6%." By late 2025 every number needs a translation layer — reported 1.8%, underlying 6% — and the translation is always in management's favor. When a management team starts asking you to look past the printed number, the printed number usually keeps getting worse first.

Second, the **capital-allocation language flipped from buyback-and-dividend to dividend-only**, justified as "continuity." That is a rationalization of a downgrade: a buyback signals "our stock is cheap"; dropping it while the stock sits near lows signals the opposite.

Third, on competition, management moved from dismissing the newcomers to *needing Germany as the proof point* — a subtle shift from "moat intact everywhere" to "look, we can win here."

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING** on the reported fundamentals and the narrative, even though the cash engine is intact.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a high-free-cash-flow, deleveraging incumbent whose reported growth has gone flat because of bank-contract losses, sitting in a payments sector the whole market is re-rating downward.** The cheapness (5.3x free cash flow) is real, but so is the reason for it — decelerating growth, a maturing secular tailwind, and a sector-wide de-rating that hit peers the same way. The load-bearing question is not "is the cash real" (it is) but "does the market ever pay a normal multiple for a payments processor again, or is the whole cohort permanently re-rated."

**Moat:** scale-cost plus switching-cost (bank distribution and embedded merchant terminals), but **ERODING** — ROIC of 1.9% is far below the cost of capital, gross margin is high (57.7%) but the reported top line is flat and bank partners are leaving. A high-but-collapsing return profile with contract attrition is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat:** **material** — stablecoin/wallet/fintech disintermediation of card take-rates plus a maturing cash-to-digital conversion. Not clearly *terminal* (European regulated acquiring is sticky and Germany shows Nexi can still win share), but a real structural cap on the terminal multiple. The cheapness is partly a sector fear-print and partly a legitimate discount for a shrinking-growth base — a hybrid, not a clean mispricing.

bull_thesis: Nexi is a cash machine priced like a melting ice cube, and the melt is slower than the price implies. The company generated 717 million euros of excess cash (its free-cash measure after capex, interest and tax) in 2024, above 800 million euros in 2025, and guides to roughly 2.4 billion euros cumulative across 2026-2028 -- against a market value of about 4.9 billion euros at today's 4.17 euros on the Milan listing. That is roughly a 16% free-cash-flow yield from an investment-grade issuer (upgraded by Fitch in December 2024 and S&P in March 2025) that cut leverage from 3.0x to 2.6x EBITDA while returning 1.1 billion euros to shareholders across 2024-25, and now pays a 0.30-euro dividend (about a 7% yield, guided to grow 5% a year). The revenue stagnation is substantially a dated, self-identified wave of Italian bank-contract losses and renegotiations that management says peaked in Q4 2025 and fades materially in the second half of 2026 -- underlying growth net of that drag ran about 6% through 2025, and Germany (merchant revenue up mid-teens in Q3 2025) and Poland prove the franchise can take share from incumbents. Conditions: the bank-contract drag must actually fade on schedule in H2 2026, the dividend must keep growing, and Germany/Poland share gains must continue.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that the discount is deserved and the rally has already spent the recovery. First, the erosion is structural, not extraordinary: Nexi's Italian distribution moat is its partner banks, and Italian banking is consolidating over Nexi's head -- Banco BPM insourced, Cassa Centrale left, renewals are repricing (the 'discontinuities' cost about 4 points of growth in 2025), the Nordic issuing client is insourcing from Q4 2025, and the MPS/Mediobanca and Credit Agricole boards are still moving. Each consolidation round converts a locked-in channel into a negotiation. Second, the March 2026 Capital Markets Day was a confession: a 3.7 billion euro goodwill impairment (the Nets/SIA roll-up overpaid), mid-single-digit growth deferred to 2028, EBIT margin expansion deferred to 2028, and -- most telling -- no buyback from a company generating 800 million euros of excess cash with its stock at an all-time low; the ten-year CEO left three weeks later. Fourth, the terminal question: account-to-account instant payments, wallets, the digital euro and stablecoin rails compress card economics over the decade, and Worldline -- the closest structural comp -- shows how far a legacy European acquirer can de-rate. consensus_delta: The street and the market disagree with each other here, and we sit between them. # NEXI.MI — Forensic Dossier (Interrogator)

**Nexi S.p.A. — Italian payments processor (merchant acquiring, card issuing, digital banking solutions). Milan listing, quoted in euros. Live price €4.173 (July 21, 2026).**
Transcript window reviewed: Q3-2024 (Nov 2024) through 9M-2025 (Nov 2025), cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory and live-verified facts through July 20, 2026.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the four calls the story is remarkably consistent in structure — and that consistency is itself the finding. Every call opens with the same three-part chant: "continued delivery of growth", "shaping Nexi for future profitable growth", "creating value for our shareholders". What changes underneath is the substance each leg carries.

- **Nov 2024 (Q3-24):** Peak confidence. Nine-month revenue up 5.6%, a deep-dive lecture on merchant-services growth drivers, and a long-term claim that the group's structural growth is "mid-to-high single digit" with merchant services "high-single digit to double digit". The cash-to-digital shift is described as running "for the very, very, very long term". Buyback accelerated and completed early.
- **Feb 2025 (FY-24):** The pivot from growth story to cash story. 2024 delivered (revenue +5.1%, margin +101bp, excess cash €717M, +19%). The heart of the call is capital allocation: first-ever dividend (€0.25/share, €300M) plus a €300M buyback — €600M total, "about 10% of the equity value of the company at current share price". Investment-grade from Fitch (and S&P in March 2025). Growth language starts leaning on "extraordinary events" — the euphemism for lost and renegotiated Italian bank contracts (Banco BPM's insourcing above all).
- **May 2025 (Q1-25):** Quiet deceleration. Revenue +3.7%, attributed to leap year and Easter. The chosen deep-dive topic is no longer growth drivers but debt and capital structure — a defensive choice of subject. Germany is the new hero market (merchant solutions +9%).
- **Nov 2025 (9M-25):** The gap becomes the story. Reported growth 2.8% for nine months, just 1.8% in the quarter; merchant solutions +0.6% in Q3. Management leans hard on an "underlying growth of about 6%" — a metric that excludes the bank losses and price renegotiations actually hitting the P&L, and which they say will peak in Q4-25 and fade only in the second half of 2026. A Capital Markets Day is promised for early March.
- **Post-transcript reality check (live-verified):** The March 5, 2026 Capital Markets Day was a reset, not a victory lap. FY-2025 closed with a net loss of about €3.4B on a roughly €3.7B non-cash goodwill impairment (normalized net profit €783M, +7.2%). The new plan pushed the return to mid-single-digit revenue growth and margin expansion out to 2028, raised the dividend 20% to €0.30/share (€350M) but scrapped the buyback. The stock fell over 20% to an all-time low of €2.643. Three weeks later (March 26, 2026) CEO Paolo Bertoluzzo — the architect of the ten-year roll-up — was replaced by his deputy Bernardo Mingrone, with three board members from the private-equity era also departing. In late April the Financial Times reported CVC Capital was weighing a ~€9B take-private, its third look at the company; the shares have since rebounded ~58% off the March low to €4.17.

The arc, in one line: a growth-and-cash narrative that progressively shed the growth leg, kept the cash leg honest, and ended with the storyteller leaving the stage.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (quarter) | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Continued delivery of growth" (every call) | Reported revenue growth: +5.6% (9M-24) → +5.1% (FY-24) → +3.7% (Q1-25) → +2.8% (9M-25) → +1.8% (Q3-25). A monotonic deceleration presented each quarter as continuity. | Narrative richer than the tape. The growth being "delivered" halved twice in a year. |
| "Underlying growth ~6%" (Nov 2025) | The 4-point gap between reported (1.8%) and "underlying" (6%) is the lost bank contracts and repricings — real, recurring revenue losses, not accounting noise. In Italy the drag is ~5 points of volume. | Adjusted-metric creep. The exclusions are the business model's central risk (bank distribution), not extraordinary items. |
| Cash generation: €717M excess cash 2024, ">€800M with a high degree of confidence" for 2025 (Nov 2025) | Delivered: 2024 €717M (+19%); FY-25 excess cash came in above €800M; TTM free cash flow €1.21B on the screener's broader definition; FCF growth +52.9% year over year. | Corroborated. The cash story is real and audited by dividends actually paid (first dividend May 21, 2025). |
| Margin expansion "at least 100bp" (2024), continued expansion 2025 | FY-24 +101bp delivered; 9M-25 +35bp — positive but a clear step down, with Q3-25 margin hit by mix and cost phasing. | Delivered in 2024, degraded in 2025. |
| "Mid-to-high single digit structural growth" long term (Nov 2024) | The March 2026 plan itself now says mid-single-digit growth only *from 2028*. | Withdrawn 16 months after being asserted. The strongest single credibility hit in the record. |
| Balance sheet: leverage 2.8x → 2.7x → 2.6x, investment grade | Confirmed by Fitch (Dec 2024) and S&P (Mar 2025) upgrades. But note the screener's Altman Z of 0.7 (formally distress-zone) — an artifact of applying a manufacturing-calibrated score to a float-heavy payments balance sheet; the rating agencies' read is the relevant one. Net-debt definitions matter here: the consolidated balance sheet shows €6.7B borrowings against €5.87B cash, but much of that cash is merchant settlement float; the company's own net financial debt is ~€4.8–5.0B (2.6x EBITDA at the November 2025 call). | Broadly corroborated, with a definitional trap for outsiders. |
| EPS: reported -2.75 (FY-25) | Driven by the ~€3.7B goodwill impairment — a formal admission that the Nets/SIA merger-era book values were inflated. Normalized EPS ~€0.66 (normalized net profit €783M on ~1.17B shares). Book value per share has compounded at -19.5%/yr over five years. | The impairment is non-cash but not meaningless: it confirms capital was destroyed at acquisition prices. The 1-of-7 quarterly beat rate (14%) squares with a management that guides to the year, not the quarter. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, with discipline.** Bertoluzzo's register moves from expansive teaching (Nov 2024's growth-driver taxonomy, drivers "really, really, really visible and strong") to procedural reassurance (Nov 2025's "we are talking about only a few million euros here and there" on the margin guide). Two tells stand out. First, the chosen deep-dive topics migrate from offense (growth drivers, Nov 2024) to defense (capital structure, May 2025). Second, the vocabulary of loss is always passive and external: contracts don't get lost, there are "extraordinary events", "discontinuities", "bank situations". Mingrone (then CFO) is consistently more concrete and quantified than the CEO — he sizes the Italian volume drag at ~5 points, names the earnout cash-outs (~€100M), and explains the volume recast. The CFO-to-CEO succession in March 2026 fits the tone record: the numbers man replaced the narrator.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** The company has a clean record on annual financial guidance: 2024 delivered on all three legs (revenue mid-single digit, margin +101bp vs "at least 100", excess cash €717M vs ">€700M"); 2025 guidance was confirmed all year and the cash leg (>€800M) was met. Sandbagging is visible in the conservative cash guides. But the *strategic* guidance — the Nov 2024 "mid-to-high single digit structural growth" frame — was effectively retracted at the March 2026 Capital Markets Day, which deferred that profile to 2028. The pattern: trust their 12-month numbers, discount their multi-year story. The 14% quarterly beat rate is consistent with guide-to-the-year behavior rather than beat-and-raise management.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Italian bank consolidation** — the single most recurring pressure point across calls (Faure, Buddhavarapu, Venturi). Analysts kept asking about Banco BPM, Cassa Centrale, Credit Agricole Italia, and MPS/Mediobanca permutations; management's answers were consistently "we are just spectators" plus relationship reassurance. This is precisely the exposure that became the 2025 revenue story. The market asked the right question two years early.
- **Sabadell/BBVA** — a serially deferred non-answer ("you're probably in a better condition than we are" to assign probability), emblematic of deal-dependent optionality that never landed.
- **The reported-vs-underlying growth bridge** (Forsythe, Nov 2025) — probing the volume recast and near-zero Q3 international-schemes growth; Mingrone conceded volumes had previously been counted more than once in places.
- **Cash balance opacity** (Leitner, Feb 2025) — how much of the ~€5.9B balance-sheet cash is actually free; the answer (~€400M minimum at holdco plus a similar amount across regulated entities, "the truth is we'll hold more cash at all times") confirms outsiders cannot cleanly compute net debt from the consolidated accounts.
- **Nordic in-sourcing** — a large Nordic issuing client's long-postponed departure finally kicking in from Q4-25; a slow-burn known loss.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The distribution moat is being eaten at the edges** — Italian bank M&A converts partner banks into lost channels (Banco BPM insourcing, Cassa Centrale); the 2025 "discontinuities" are this risk crystallizing, and the Italian bank-consolidation board is still in motion (Q3-25 call).
🔴 **€3.7B goodwill impairment (FY-25)** — formal confirmation the Nets/SIA roll-up overpaid; five-year book-value-per-share growth of -19.5%/yr.
🔴 **Growth story retracted** — the March 2026 plan pushes mid-single-digit growth to 2028; Q3-25 merchant solutions grew 0.6% reported.
🔴 **Leadership rupture after ten years** — CEO out three weeks after a plan the market rejected with a -20% single-day move; three private-equity-linked directors out simultaneously.
🔴 **Adjusted-metric creep** — "underlying growth" excludes recurring contract losses; volumes were recast mid-stream.
🟢 **Cash generation is real and improving** — €400M → €600M → €717M → >€800M excess-cash progression, trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of €1.21B (+52.9% year over year); dividends actually paid.
🟢 **Deleveraging delivered** — 3.0x → 2.6x while returning €1.1B to shareholders across 2024–25; double investment-grade upgrade.
🟢 **Germany and Poland are genuine share-gain stories** — German merchant solutions up 9% (Q1-25) accelerating to mid-teens (Q3-25), won from local incumbents while exiting unprofitable volume.
🟢 **Cost control is credible** — costs +0.8% (Q1-25), ~2% (9M-25) against mid-single-digit underlying revenue growth; the operating-leverage machine works.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling subtle shift is what happened to the buyback. Nov 2024: buyback accelerated and completed early, framed as conviction. Feb 2025: €300M buyback alongside the first dividend. March 2026 (post-transcript): buyback gone entirely, dividend raised instead — with the stated logic that a dividend signals "continuity" while a buyback "may or may not be there". A company whose stock hit an all-time low choosing *not* to buy it back — while generating more than €800M of yearly excess cash — is either preserving flexibility for the leverage target, or telling you the board does not consider the shares obviously cheap relative to its own uncertainty. Second signal: the earnout admission (Nov 2024) that ~€100M of acquisition earnouts sit in net debt — small, but a reminder the roll-up's liabilities linger. Third: the Planet partnership and the 500-partner ISV count are progress markers that never translate into disclosed revenue — narrative filler. Fourth: Mingrone's precision as CFO (naming drags, sizing losses) reads as a green flag for the new CEO era; his first strategic act, however, was to lengthen the timeline and cut the buyback — realism over promotion.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** The ten-year roll-up era ended in a single month (impairment + plan reset + CEO change, March 2026). The cash engine is genuine — this is now roughly a 16% free-cash-flow-yield payments utility paying a ~7% dividend yield — but the growth narrative that justified the old multiple has been formally deferred to 2028, and the transition is being run by a new chief executive on a plan the market initially rejected.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** whether the Italian bank-channel erosion is a passing wave of contract discontinuities (management's claim — fading materially in the second half of 2026) or the beginning of permanent distribution decay as Italian banking consolidates. Everything else — the multiple, the dividend capacity, the CVC interest — hangs off that answer. Note also that the current price (€4.17) already sits ~58% above the March low and above the sell-side consensus target (~€3.7–3.9), largely on a private-equity approach that is non-binding, politically gated, and opposed by the second-largest shareholder (CDP, 19.1%).

**Moat assessment:** The moat is a combination of scale-cost advantage (processing scale across Europe) and switching costs via entrenched bank partnerships — real but **narrow**, and the bank-distribution leg is demonstrably eroding: partner banks are consolidating, insourcing (Banco BPM, the large Nordic client), and repricing renewals. Returns evidence agrees: return on invested capital of ~1.9% sits below any reasonable cost of capital, and book value is shrinking even as gross margin expands. The EBITDA margin (north of 50%, still expanding modestly) shows the processing-scale leg is intact; the erosion is in the distribution leg — the trend is negative even though the core utility endures.

**Secular threat:** Material but not terminal. Account-to-account instant payments, wallets, and stablecoin rails threaten the card take-rate over a decade — the classic fintech-disintermediation tail — and the digital euro looms as a policy variant. Offsetting it, Nexi's core markets (Italy, Germany, Poland, Greece) still run 1–2 points a year of cash-to-digital conversion, a tailwind management credibly documents. The cheapness at the March low was mostly a fear-print; at today's rebounded price the residual discount is thinner and part of the earnings base is structurally contested. This is a narrow-moat cash machine priced between those two truths.

bull_thesis: Nexi is a cash machine priced like a melting ice cube, and the melt is slower than the price implies. The company generated 717 million euros of excess cash (its free-cash measure after capex, interest and tax) in 2024, above 800 million euros in 2025, and guides to roughly 2.4 billion euros cumulative across 2026-2028 -- against a market value of about 4.9 billion euros at today's 4.17 euros on the Milan listing. That is roughly a 16% free-cash-flow yield from an investment-grade issuer (upgraded by Fitch in December 2024 and S&P in March 2025) that cut leverage from 3.0x to 2.6x EBITDA while returning 1.1 billion euros to shareholders across 2024-25, and now pays a 0.30-euro dividend (about a 7% yield, guided to grow 5% a year). The revenue stagnation is substantially a dated, self-identified wave of Italian bank-contract losses and renegotiations that management says peaked in Q4 2025 and fades materially in the second half of 2026 -- underlying growth net of that drag ran about 6% through 2025, and Germany (merchant revenue up mid-teens in Q3 2025) and Poland prove the franchise can take share from incumbents. The March 2026 reset (3.7 billion euro goodwill impairment, growth deferred to 2028, no buyback) crushed the stock to 2.64 euros and cleared the deck: a new operator-CEO (Bernardo Mingrone, the long-time CFO), conservative targets, and a valuation so low that CVC Capital -- for the third time -- is weighing a take-private reported at about 9 billion euros (FT, April 28, 2026). Even if no bid lands, the sum of the parts on distressed-cohort multiples less the company-defined net financial debt supports roughly 5.20 euros per share; delivery of the 2028 growth inflection or any formal offer takes it toward 6.80. Conditions: the bank-contract drag must actually fade on schedule in H2 2026, the dividend must keep growing, and Germany/Poland share gains must continue.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that the discount is deserved and the rally has already spent the recovery. First, the erosion is structural, not extraordinary: Nexi's Italian distribution moat is its partner banks, and Italian banking is consolidating over Nexi's head -- Banco BPM insourced, Cassa Centrale left, renewals are repricing (the 'discontinuities' cost about 4 points of growth in 2025), the Nordic issuing client is insourcing from Q4 2025, and the MPS/Mediobanca and Credit Agricole boards are still moving. Each consolidation round converts a locked-in channel into a negotiation. Second, the March 2026 Capital Markets Day was a confession: a 3.7 billion euro goodwill impairment (the Nets/SIA roll-up overpaid), mid-single-digit growth deferred to 2028, EBIT margin expansion deferred to 2028, and -- most telling -- no buyback from a company generating 800 million euros of excess cash with its stock at an all-time low; the ten-year CEO left three weeks later. Third, the price has already run: 4.17 euros is 58% above the March low and sits ABOVE the sell-side consensus target of roughly 3.7-3.9 euros, with the gap plausibly the CVC premium -- yet the approach is early-stage, described as 'entirely political', opposed by CDP (the 19.1% second shareholder, which does not want a delisting), gated by Italy's golden-power veto, and it is CVC's third look with no bid after the first two. If CVC walks, the event money exits and the stock likely retraces toward the mid-3s. Fourth, the terminal question: account-to-account instant payments, wallets, the digital euro and stablecoin rails compress card economics over the decade, and Worldline -- the closest structural comp -- shows how far a legacy European acquirer can de-rate. Confirmation signs: H1 2026 (July 29) showing the drag NOT fading as promised, another bank loss announced, CVC formally passing, or the dividend growth path softening.
consensus_delta: The street and the market disagree with each other here, and we sit between them. The sell-side consensus target is about 3.7-3.9 euros (MarketScreener ~3.71 across 18 analysts; Investing.com ~3.81-3.86; a smaller TipRanks sample at 5.27) — BELOW the current 4.17 price. So the tape is not pricing the analysts' fundamental view; it is pricing a partial take-private premium on a non-binding, thrice-attempted, politically gated approach. Where the street is wrong, in our view: valuing a business that reliably converts more than 800 million euros a year into distributable cash at roughly 4.5-4.7x that cash flow assumes the bank-contract erosion is permanent AND accelerating, when the drag is substantially dated (management sized it, said it peaks in Q4 2025, and Italy's bank-consolidation wave has a finite roster of remaining contracts) and the underlying engine grew about 6% with mid-teens German share gains. Our sum-of-the-parts of about 5.20 euros says the equity is worth roughly 25% more than today's price WITHOUT any bid. Where the market is wrong: treating CVC interest as a floor. CDP's opposition plus golden power make this the hardest kind of deal to close in Italy, and two prior CVC looks produced nothing. Both errors can be true at once — which is exactly why the entry price, not the thesis, is the decision variable.
forcing_function: Dated events, in order: July 29, 2026 — first-half results and the new chief executive's first outing; the specific thing to listen for is confirmation that the bank-contract drag is fading on schedule into H2 (the entire 2028 plan rests on it) and any capital-allocation hint about resuming buybacks. Second half of 2026 — the guided inflection window itself: Q3/Q4 prints (early November 2026, late February 2027) must show reported growth converging toward the ~6% underlying rate; that convergence, not any single event, is what forces the fundamental re-rate toward 5+ euros. March 2027 — full-year results plus the 2027 capital-allocation decision (the company holds about 1.3 billion euros of flexibility for deleveraging, small M&A, or returns; a buyback reinstatement at these prices would be the strongest possible signal). Undated but live: any formal CVC offer, Rome golden-power signal, or CDP position change — binary in both directions. And structurally: each Italian bank-M&A resolution (MPS/Mediobanca, Credit Agricole Italia) removes or confirms a piece of the bear case. There is no contractual, binding event with a fixed payout on the calendar — which is precisely why this is a wait-for-the-price name rather than an aggressive-entry special situation.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months hold four specific hazards. (1) July 29, 2026: the first-half report, the new chief executive's first print, lands in the single most crowded macro window of the year (July 28-29 Federal Reserve meeting, the big-tech capital-spending verdicts July 29-30, June inflation data July 30) — per our regime read, catalysts resolving inside that cluster get muted or delayed re-rates, and negative surprises travel farther than positive ones with positioning this full. The quarter itself still carries near-peak bank-contract drag (the fade is guided to the SECOND half of 2026), so the reported growth number will look ugly even on plan. (2) The CVC premium can evaporate on a single headline: a formal pass, a golden-power signal from Rome, or CDP restating its opposition likely retraces the stock toward the mid-3-euro area where it traded before the April 28 report. (3) The macro overlay is hostile to leveraged euro consumer-payments names in the tail: a second Hormuz oil shock is live (Brent about 89 dollars), a December Fed hike is the priced base case, and European consumer spending is the volume engine — a spending stall would hit the 'underlying 6%' claim directly. (4) Residual Italian bank M&A: any new insourcing announcement from the MPS/Mediobanca or Credit Agricole complexes would confirm the bear's structural-erosion read and reset the 2028 plan again. Nothing here threatens solvency — 2.6x levered, investment grade, maturities being paid from cash — the risk is to the equity narrative, not the balance sheet.
positioning_washout: Most of the washout already happened, which is the honest reason the stock could rally 58% in four months. The March 5 Capital-Markets-Day collapse (down more than 20% in a day to 2.643 euros, an all-time low) forcibly cleared the growth-at-a-reasonable-price holders who had owned the old mid-single-digit story, and the ten-year CEO's exit plus three private-equity-linked board departures ended the legacy-sponsor overhang narrative that had capped the stock for years (the old Advent/Bain/Hellman blocks have been distributing since 2023). What replaced them: income buyers (7% growing dividend), deep-value funds, and — since April 28 — event-driven money positioned for a CVC bid. That last cohort is the fragile layer: it is renting, not owning, and exits mechanically on a deal-death headline, which is what a fall back toward the pre-report mid-3s would be. There is no index-exclusion or forced-selling mechanic pending; CDP's 19.1% strategic stake is immovable and actually shrinks the effective float. Net: the register is cleaner than it has been in years, but the marginal buyer today is the least committed one.
moderator_conclusion: Verdict: wait for the wash-out — the thesis is real, the price is not yet paying you for its risks. Nexi at 4.17 euros is a narrow-moat payments utility generating more than 800 million euros of annual distributable cash (about a 16% cash yield, 7% dividend) whose sum of the parts on already-distressed multiples is worth about 5.20 euros — but the 25% discount is the THIN version of this opportunity. The market offered the FAT version twice this year (2.64 in March, 3.47 in mid-May), and what closed the gap since was not fundamental delivery but a soft, non-binding private-equity approach that the second-largest shareholder opposes and Rome can veto — the third such approach, with the prior two dying quietly. Our regime read argues for exactly this discipline: it rewards hard-dated catalysts and penalizes soft extended ones, and Nexi's only dated event (July 29 results) lands inside the year's most crowded macro window carrying near-peak drag optics, with a full-positioning tape in which negative surprises travel farther than positive ones. The forensic record adds a second reason to demand a discount: a 3.7 billion euro impairment, a growth promise retracted at the March plan, adjusted-metric creep, and a board that declined to buy back its own all-time-low stock. So: do not chase the bid premium. The committee's entry is either (a) a deal-death or macro flush back toward 3.30-3.50 euros — roughly the mid-May level, where downside to the 2.90 adverse case is modest against 50%-plus upside to fair value — or (b) evidence at the July 29 or Q3 print that the bank-contract drag is genuinely fading, which would justify paying up for the fundamental path. On the value question alone, ignoring all catalyst and timing considerations: this is a real cash machine at a genuine discount, but the moat's distribution leg is visibly eroding as Italian banks consolidate and payments disintermediation advances, and that erosion caps how hard we will ever press this name — a low multiple on a structurally contested base is only conditionally cheap. A three on both dials: a fair thesis at an unfair entry.
sop_breakdown: Base case, FY-2025 actuals (EBITDA ~1.9B euros, net revenues ~3.6B): Merchant Solutions ~1.05B EBITDA at 6.5x = 6.8B; Issuing Solutions ~0.6B at 5.5x = 3.3B; Digital Banking Solutions ~0.25B at 5.5x = 1.4B (CDP carve-out interest supports the mark). Enterprise value ~11.5B euros. Less net financial debt ~4.8B -- the COMPANY definition (~2.6x EBITDA per the November 2025 call), deliberately used instead of the recomputed 917M (838M ex-lease) figure because the 5.87B of consolidated cash is largely merchant settlement float and regulatory minimums (the CFO conceded ~800M+ is structurally locked and 'the truth is we'll hold more cash at all times'); treating float as free cash would fabricate ~3 euros per share of phantom value. Equity ~6.7B over ~1.17B shares = ~5.70; haircut ~10% for forensic quality (impairment history, adjusted-metric creep, guidance reset) = ~5.20 euros. Cross-check: 800M excess cash at 7.5x = 6.0B equity = ~5.10 -- the two methods agree.
risk_reward: From 4.17 euros: downside to the adverse case at 2.90 (the level the market actually printed in March 2026 when the plan disappointed, and roughly where the stock would settle if CVC walks away); upside to the base sum-of-the-parts at 5.20 on delivery of the H2-2026 drag fade, with 6.80 if the 2028 growth inflection lands or a formal bid emerges. The entry math was far better at the May price of 3.47 than it is after the speculative rally.
peer_comps_note: The peer file reads Nexi at 5.9x price-to-free-cash-flow as in line with its cohort: far below Adyen (30-40x, the quality premium Nexi lacks) and Global Payments (~10-12x), and inside Worldline's post-scandal distressed band (~5-8x) — the closest structural analog as a fellow European legacy-acquirer roll-up. That placement means the headline cheapness is largely a sector-wide de-rating of legacy European payments (shared repricing risk from bank insourcing and fintech disintermediation) plus name-specific quality issues (negative reported net margin from the impairment, ROIC ~1.9%, distress-zone Altman Z artifact), NOT pure idiosyncratic mispricing. The sum-of-the-parts multiples used here (4.5-7x EV/EBITDA) deliberately anchor to the current de-rated cohort, not to pre-2022 payments multiples.
